strengths: Novel investigation of endogenous steering resistance phenomenon with rigorous experimental methodology, including no-steering baseline control (0% multi-attempt across 7,892 trials), random latent ablation control, and threshold calibration via Probabilistic Bisection Algorithm

Strong cross-judge validation across 5 independent models (90-96% agreement on multi-attempt detection and improvement scoring) from different providers, providing robust evidence against evaluation bias

Mechanistic insights using SAE latents: identifies 26 differentially-activated latents with causal contribution (27% ESR reduction via ablation) and sequential activation analysis showing OTD latents fire 4.4× higher during off-topic regions
Comprehensive supplementary materials with detailed hyperparameters, judge prompts, meta-prompt variants, and multi-ratio fine-tuning analysis supporting reproducibility and transparency
Honest treatment of limitations, explicitly acknowledging 25% unexplained effect, inability to isolate scale vs. architecture vs. training, and constraints of single-layer SAE analysis
weaknesses: Severely limited generalization: ESR phenomenon substantial only in Llama-3.3-70B (3.8%) with all other 4 models <1%, preventing definitive isolation of whether effects reflect model scale, architecture, or training procedures; testing across only 2 model families raises generalizability concerns

Post-hoc layer selection introduces experimental bias: for Llama-3.3-70B, steering applied at layer 33 optimized for 'higher-quality results'; for Gemma-2-27B, explicitly selected layer 22 based on 'highest ESR incidence'—optimizing for most favorable outcomes rather than predetermined protocol

Mechanistic understanding is partial (25% of ESR reduction unexplained) with concerning heterogeneity: approximately half of 26 'off-topic detector' latents show negative effect sizes (higher activation during on-topic content), contradicting functional labels and suggesting incoherent circuit interpretation

Fine-tuning results fundamentally undermine interpretation: successfully induces behavioral multi-attempt pattern in smaller models but effectiveness (improvement rate) remains flat, suggesting surface pattern learning rather than genuine monitoring capability—raises serious question whether baseline Llama-3.3-70B ESR is similarly superficial

Limited prompt coverage with narrow domain: only 38 'explain how' prompts with similar format/complexity; no testing on creative tasks, reasoning, code, or safety-critical steering targets; unclear if ESR manifests with diverse prompt distributions

Missing critical safety-relevant analyses: no evaluation of ESR when steering toward harmful content, no interaction analysis with other steering methods (LEACE, representation engineering), no testing of interference with genuine safety interventions despite speculation in discussion

Causality framing overstates evidence: ablation establishes necessity for identified latents but not sufficiency; 27% reduction could reflect redundant circuits with incomplete ablation rather than causal drivers; use of 'causal evidence' throughout is technically imprecise

Evaluation metric limitations: ESR measured exclusively by explicit self-correction phrases, missing all implicit corrections; judge-based scoring is inherently subjective; cross-judge agreement percentages evaluated on stratified sample deliberately oversampling multi-attempt cases (not population-representative)

strengths: Novel phenomenon with systematic empirical characterization using well-designed controls (no-steering baseline, cross-judge validation, matched random ablation)
Rigorous causal evidence through SAE latent ablation showing 27% reduction in ESR rate; control experiments confirm specificity to identified latents
Clear presentation with effective figures and comprehensive appendix; sequential activation analysis shows plausible temporal patterns consistent with monitoring
Practical insights on enhancing ESR through meta-prompting (4.3× increase) with scale-dependent effects
Strong inter-judge agreement (90-96%) across 5 different LLM judges, validating evaluation robustness
weaknesses: Severe generality limitation: ESR substantially present in only 1 of 5 models (3.8% for Llama-3.3-70B vs ≤1% for others); cannot disentangle scale, architecture, or training effects; may be model-specific

Fine-tuning results directly contradict core interpretation: fine-tuning increases multi-attempt rate but NOT success rate, suggesting learned behavioral pattern rather than genuine internal monitoring circuits
Only 25-27% ESR reduction from ablating 26 latents indicates incomplete mechanistic explanation; ~50% of identified latents show wrong expected pattern (negative effect sizes)

Methodological concerns: post-hoc layer selection based on favorable outcomes; SAE trained on layer 50 but steering applied at layer 33; same prompts used for latent identification and ESR evaluation (overfitting risk)
Temporal activation patterns are correlational; authors acknowledge temporal precedence doesn't establish causality at single-episode level; interpretation as 'monitoring circuits' is inferential
Safety implications are dual and unresolved: paper mentions ESR could protect OR interfere with beneficial steering but provides no empirical evidence on safety-relevant steering interventions
Limited scope: only 5 models across 2 families, 38 'explain-how' prompts, only SAE additive steering tested; unclear if results generalize to other task types or interventions

strengths: Novel and well-motivated phenomenon: ESR is a genuinely interesting observation about model introspection and internal consistency-checking with clear relevance to interpretability and AI alignment

Rigorous experimental methodology: Strong control experiment (0% multi-attempt without steering across 7,892 trials), robust cross-judge validation (5 LLMs with 90-96% agreement), appropriate causal controls (random latent ablation), and per-latent threshold calibration

Multi-faceted investigation: Examines ESR from multiple angles including characterization across models, mechanistic latent identification, prompting effects, fine-tuning, and sequential activation analysis

Interpretability contribution: Identifies 26 differentially-activated latents with compelling evidence (4.4× elevation during off-topic content, activation preceding verbal correction) for mechanistic involvement in self-correction

Clear presentation and honest limitations: Well-organized paper with excellent visualizations, comprehensive 24-page appendices, and transparent discussion of constraints from single-layer SAEs, limited model coverage, and evaluation methodology
Thoughtful implications discussion: Nuanced analysis of dual nature of ESR (protection against manipulation vs. interference with safety interventions) with appropriate framing of tradeoffs
weaknesses: Limited generalization and scale confound: ESR is primarily a Llama-3.3-70B phenomenon with only 5 models tested across 2 families; cannot disentangle scale, architecture, and training effects; near-absence in all Gemma models suggests potential Llama-specificity

Incomplete mechanistic explanation: Ablating 26 latents reduces multi-attempt rate by only 25%, leaving ~75% unexplained; heterogeneous latent effects (~half activate during off-topic, half during on-topic) suggest broader coherence-monitoring roles; single-layer analysis cannot trace complete computational circuits

Fine-tuning dissociation poorly resolved: Fine-tuning induces behavioral pattern (more attempts) but NOT improved effectiveness—this striking dissociation raises fundamental questions about whether learned behavior represents genuine monitoring vs. surface imitation, addressed but not deeply explained

Evaluation limitations risk overfitting: Same prompt set used for both latent identification and ESR evaluation could inflate estimates; narrow domain (38 pedagogical 'explain how' prompts); only explicit self-correction captured; no evaluation on safety-critical steering targets

Safety analysis remains speculative: Interesting discussion of ESR interfering with alignment techniques but NO empirical testing of whether ESR undermines safety interventions; claims about protection against adversarial attacks unvalidated

Methodological choices introduce concerns: Post-hoc layer selection based on 'best performing' criterion (Gemma-2-27B); Llama-3.3-70B steered at layer 33 vs. SAE training layer 50; relevance/concreteness filtering reduces latent pool to 50% potentially biasing selection

Limited investigation of prompting enhancement: Only 6 meta-prompt variants tested; successful variant quite specific; sensitivity to wording not systematically explored; underlying mechanisms of size-dependent scaling not deeply investigated

Reproducibility concerns: Dependence on proprietary Goodfire Ember API for latent identification; code availability not mentioned; GemmaScope SAEs trained on pretrained (not instruction-tuned) models creates confound

strengths: Novel phenomenon: Identifies and operationalizes Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR), demonstrating that language models can spontaneously recover from steering-induced perturbations with explicit self-correction. This is a genuinely interesting behavior with implications for interpretability and alignment.

Rigorous experimental design: Comprehensive controls including no-steering baseline (0% multi-attempt over 7,892 trials), random-latent ablation, held-out prompt validation (30-45% reduction on 20 new prompts), and cross-judge validation across 5 independent LLMs with 90-96% agreement. Sampling strategy appropriately accounts for oversampling multi-attempt cases.

Thoughtful mechanistic decomposition: Prefilling control convincingly separates detection (text-conditioned) from sustained resistance. Matched-prefix experiment (Section 3.7) shows natural post-correction text improves 2.1x more than matched on-topic prefix (p<0.001), indicating mechanism beyond simple autoregressive conditioning. Sequential activation analysis provides supporting evidence with 4.4x higher activation during off-topic regions.

Identification of associated latents: Contrastive search yields 26 interpretable SAE features; ablation shows causal contribution (27% reduction from 3.8% to 2.8%) with specificity confirmed by random-latent control. Temporal dynamics align with proposed functional role.

Excellent reproducibility: Code released, 28-page appendix with full experimental protocols, judge prompts, hyperparameters, and supplementary experiments. Threshold calibration and all 38 prompts documented. Cross-model judge validation demonstrates robustness of findings.

Honest limitations discussion: Authors clearly acknowledge inability to disentangle scale/architecture/training, heterogeneous latent effects, metric narrowness (explicit only), and limited generalization across steering paradigms.

Practical insights: Shows ESR can be enhanced through meta-prompting (4.3x increase) and provides evidence that behavioral imitation via fine-tuning does not install effective monitoring, informing future training methodology research.
weaknesses: Severely limited scope: ESR robustly observed only in Llama-3.3-70B at 3.8%; all other tested models show <1%. Cannot disentangle whether this is scale, architecture, or training difference. Raises fundamental question of whether this is general property or model-specific quirk, limiting generalizability.

Metric narrowness and potential underestimation: Captures only explicit verbal self-correction; implicit recovery unmeasured. Holistic judge for detecting gradual shifts systemically overscores (judge mean 8.2 vs. human 3.3), suggesting the paper may miss the broader phenomenon by 10-100x. This design choice prioritizes precision at cost of completeness.

Latent heterogeneity undermines circuit narrative: 26 identified latents show mixed polarity with only ~50% showing expected positive Cohen's d pattern. Roughly half show opposite or insignificant patterns (Table 3), and ~half of labels describe discourse/repair rather than detection. Ablating both positive- and negative-d subsets equally reduces ESR (Appendix A.3.5), suggesting complex mechanism or potential artifacts that weakens 'detector' interpretation despite causal ablation effect.

Sustained resistance mechanism only ~50% explained: Matched-prefix experiment shows recent on-topic context explains only ~50% of post-correction quality improvement (+21.8 vs. +45.8). Remaining 50% attributed to three competing explanations with no decisive evidence for any. Central ESR mechanism remains partially opaque.

Moderate absolute effect sizes: 3.8% ESR rate is low in absolute terms; latent ablation reduces by only 27% (3.8%→2.8%), leaving 73% unexplained. Meta-prompting effects large (4.3x) but suggest behavioral imitation rather than genuine monitoring. Limits real-world safety implications.

Limited generalization of steering paradigm: Tests only additive residual-stream steering (SAE-derived and Wikipedia-derived). No testing of logit-space steering, attention head edits, multi-layer interventions, or probe-based steering. Generalizability across steering types incompletely characterized.

Safety implications underdeveloped: Dual implications noted (hardening vs. interference) but not empirically explored. No experiments testing ESR against actual adversarial attacks or existing safety interventions (e.g., Representation Engineering, Inference-Time Intervention). Safety significance remains theoretical.

Limited theoretical understanding: Primarily empirical/descriptive work. No mechanistic explanation for why ESR emerges, scaling relationship unclear, and fundamental question unanswered: what training process induces this capability and why is it weak in 8B but strong in 70B models?

Fine-tuning experiment limited scope: Only one model fine-tuned; synthetic data from Claude; no fine-tuning under active steering (acknowledged gap). Loss masking strategy may artificially constrain what's learnable. Result that behavioral imitation ≠ sustained effectiveness is somewhat expected.

Edge case statistics: Smaller models' improvement rates based on very few multi-attempt episodes (n=5 for Gemma-2-2B), with authors acknowledging unreliability. Post-hoc layer selection for Llama-3.3-70B (layer 33 vs. 50 based on ESR incidence) raises reproducibility questions.

strengths: Rigorous experimental controls including no-steering baseline, prefilling dissociation, matched-prefix comparison, random ablation, held-out prompt validation, and cross-judge agreement across 5 independent judges (90-96%)—demonstrating genuine care for soundness

Honest and transparent treatment of limitations: authors clearly acknowledge heterogeneous latent patterns (~50% unexpected), inability to disentangle scale/architecture/training, metric narrowness, failed holistic judge, and 50% unexplained post-correction improvement

Well-designed per-latent threshold calibration, large trial counts (thousands per model), multiple metrics (multi-attempt rate, improvement rate, ESR rate), and extensive methodological transparency in appendices with promised code availability
Interesting phenomenon worthy of investigation: ESR provides a novel lens on apparent model self-monitoring and coherence detection during generation
weaknesses: Scale-dependent phenomenon with unexplained gap: ESR only manifests clearly in Llama-3.3-70B (3.8%); all other models tested show <1%; authors explicitly cannot disentangle whether gap reflects scale, architecture, or training differences, severely limiting generalizability claims

Weak mechanistic understanding undermining circuit identification: ~50% of 26 identified latents activate more during on-topic content (negative d), contradicting off-topic-detector narrative; ablation reduces ESR only 27%; both positive-d and negative-d subsets reduce ESR equally, indicating compositional mechanism not cleanly characterized; authors' own caveat: 'stop short of claiming a clean monitoring circuit'

Metric narrowness with implicit recovery unmeasured: explicit-restart metric is by design narrow; alternative holistic judge failed blind human validation (judge scored 3.3/10 where humans scored 8.2/10), revealing this metric may capture atypical surface pattern rather than true coherence monitoring

Prefilling control produces puzzling results: unsteered model with off-topic prefix self-corrects 7-13.5% vs. 2-3% under active steering, suggesting active steering inhibits rather than facilitates correction—opposite to internal-monitoring hypothesis; proposed explanation is post-hoc and untested

Matched-prefix experiment leaves ~50% of post-correction quality unexplained with multiple unfalsifiable candidate mechanisms (specific corrective phrasing, latent recruitment, steering-signal suppression); no follow-up experiments distinguish these explanations

Fine-tuning experiment is negative for mechanistic claims: increased multi-attempt rate but unchanged success rate demonstrates training installs surface behavior without underlying capability, suggesting ESR may reflect stylistic pattern-matching rather than genuine monitoring

Post-hoc layer selection for Llama-3.3-70B (layer 33 vs. trained layer 50) justified by 'higher-quality results' and 'more interpretable ESR behavior'—selection based on desired outcome before ablation experiments introduces potential bias

Narrow experimental domain: only 38 'explain how' prompts (math, housekeeping, business); no tests on reasoning tasks, code generation, creative writing, multi-turn dialogue, or adversarial examples; results may not generalize beyond narrow educational instruction domain

Limited steering paradigm: only residual-stream additive single-layer interventions; no logit-space, attention head, multi-layer, or probe-based steering; Wikipedia-vector validation (n=278) overlaps confidence intervals with SAE baseline; generalization remains open

Alignment implications underdeveloped: dual-use concerns identified but not empirically tested; no validation that ESR actually defends against adversarial attacks or interferes with beneficial steering; meta-prompting 'lightweight defensive intervention' claim untested against adversarial scenarios

strengths: Novel characterization of endogenous steering resistance (ESR)—a previously unreported phenomenon where models spontaneously recover from adversarial activation steering. First systematic study of this behavior

Rigorous experimental design with comprehensive controls: no-steering baseline, boost-level ablations, random-latent controls, held-out prompt validation, Wikipedia-derived vectors, and prefilling/matched-prefix controls that cleanly decompose detection from sustained resistance
Strong inter-judge agreement (90-96%) across five independent judge models (GPT-4-mini, Qwen3, Claude, Gemini) validates robustness of ESR rate and multi-attempt detection

Mechanistic insights via causal intervention: 26 identified latents reduce ESR by 25-27% (with random-latent and held-out-prompt controls supporting specificity). Sequential activation analysis shows these latents fire 4.4× higher during off-topic regions

Matched-prefix experiment provides novel evidence that sustained resistance isn't fully text-conditioned: natural post-correction text outperforms length-matched on-topic prefix by 2.1×, indicating genuine post-correction mechanism beyond conditioning

Comprehensive reproducibility support: code release commitment, full judge prompts in appendices, detailed hyperparameters (Table 7), and 28-page appendix with supplementary experiments, latent statistics, and methodological details

Honest and thorough limitations discussion (Section 5.1): acknowledges metric scope (explicit restarts only), inability to disentangle scale/architecture/training, latent heterogeneity, and incomplete fine-tuning experiments. Builds credibility through transparency
Clear presentation with effective visualizations: Figures 2, 7, and 8 communicate findings well. Two-component decomposition (detection vs. sustained resistance) elegantly frames complex phenomena
weaknesses: Narrow phenomenon scope severely limits generalizability: ESR occurs in only 3.8% of Llama-3.3-70B responses (the only model showing substantial rates), while all other tested models show <1%. Cannot determine whether gap reflects model scale, architecture, or training differences. Single-model mechanistic findings may not transfer

Incomplete mechanistic understanding: matched-prefix experiment explains only ~50% of post-correction quality improvement; remaining 50% has multiple unresolved candidate explanations. Weakens causal claims about underlying resistance mechanism

Identified 26 'self-correction-associated latents' are heterogeneous: ~50% show expected off-topic detector patterns, ~50% show opposite or near-zero effects. Authors appropriately revise terminology from 'off-topic detectors' but acknowledge these don't form a cleanly characterized circuit. Limits interpretability claims

Limited steering paradigm coverage: only tests additive residual-stream perturbations at single layer. Wikipedia-vector validation rules out SAE-specific artifacts but doesn't establish generality across logit-space, attention head edits, multi-layer interventions, or probe-based steering. ESR's prevalence under other methods unknown

Fine-tuning experiment is incomplete single recipe (Llama-3.1-8B): key condition not tested is fine-tuning under active steering. Finding that training increases attempt rate but not success rate remains ambiguous—could indicate surface behavior learning or indicate ceiling effects rather than insight into actual monitoring capability

Explicit-restart evaluation metric is intentionally narrow and will completely miss implicit/non-verbalized recovery. Developed holistic judge for gradual shifts but found it systematically over-scores these cases (judge mean 8.2 vs. human 3.3), leaving true rate of implicit ESR unmeasured

Post-hoc layer selection for Llama-3.3-70B: steering applied at layer 33 despite SAE trained on layer 50. Selection justified post-hoc as producing 'higher-quality results'—acknowledged as potential source of bias, though occurred before main ablation experiments

Limited prompt diversity: 38 'explain how' prompts on instructional topics. Unclear whether ESR transfers to other task families (reasoning, creative writing, dialogue, safety-critical tasks). Held-out prompts test new domains but remain within instructional category
